﻿ Node .js Node.js is a runtime environment that allows us to execute JavaScript code outside a web browser.
Normally, JavaScript runs inside browsers like Chrome or Firefox. With Node.js, JavaScript can also run on a server or computer.
Node.js is mainly used to develop the backend of web applications.
It is built on Google Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine, which makes JavaScript execution fast.
Node.js is open-source and cross-platform, so it can run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
It uses an event-driven and non-blocking architecture, allowing it to handle many requests efficiently.

﻿ Asynchronous programming  Asynchronous programming allows Node.js to perform tasks without waiting for one task to finish before starting another.
Node.js starts a time-consuming operation, such as reading a file or accessing a database. 
It continues executing the remaining code. 
When the operation finishes, its result is handled using a callback, Promise, or async/await. 
This non-blocking approach helps Node.js handle many requests efficiently.

It is called at the completion of each task. 
All APIs of Node are written in a way to supports callbacks. 
For example: when a function start reading file, it returns the control to execution environment immediately so that the next instruction can be executed.
Once file I/O is complete, it will call the callback function. 
No blocking or wait for File I/O. 
It can process high number of request without waiting for any function to return result.

﻿ Event loops      The event loop allows Node.js to perform tasks without blocking or stopping the execution of other code.
The event loop allows Node.js to perform non-blocking I/O operations. 
Most operating systems are multithreaded. 
Node.js is single-threaded. 
After completion of an operation, the kernel informs Node.js, and the respective callback is added to the event queue, where it will eventually be executed.

﻿ Features of Event Loop Event loop is an endless loop, which waits for tasks, executes them and then 	sleeps until it receives more tasks. The event loop executes tasks from the 	empty i.e. there is no ongoing task. event queue only when the call stack is callbacks The event loop allows us to use	and promises. The event loop executes the tasks starting from the oldest first.

﻿ Phases of Event Loop o timers: this phase executes callbacks scheduled by setTimeout() and setInterval().
o pending callbacks: executes I/O callbacks deferred to the next loop iteration.
o idle, prepare: only used internally (This is mainly internal Node.js work.)
o poll: retrieve new I/O events; execute I/O related callbacks (almost all with the exception of close callbacks, the ones scheduled by timers, and setImmediate()); node will block here when appropriate.
o check: setImmediate() callbacks are invoked here.
o close callbacks: some close callbacks, e.g. socket.on('close', ...). (works inside the Node.js runtime)

﻿ Buffers The Buffer class in Node.js is designed to handle raw binary data.
A temporary memory area that stores binary data
Fixed size: it cannot grow or shrink after creation
Global object: no require() needed
Each element is one byte (a value from 0 to 255)

Why do we need Buffers?
JavaScript originally had no way to handle binary data.
Needed for: file reading, network requests, streams, images, video, encryption
Data arrives in chunks, so Node needs a place to hold each chunk

       When using console.log() to print the Buffer instance, you'll get a chain of values in hexadecimal values.

﻿ Streams Streams are Objects that let you read data from a source or write data to a
destination in continuous fashion, instead of loading all the data at once.

In Node.js, there are four types of streams −
Readable −  Stream which is used for read operation.
Writable −  Stream which is used for write operation.
Duplex −  Stream which can be used for both read and write operation.
Transform −  A type of duplex stream where the output is computed based 	on input.

﻿ Streams Each type of Stream is an EventEmitter instance and throws several events at 	different instance of times.
  (A Stream is also an EventEmitter, so it generates events at different times.)
commonly used events −
data − This event is fired when there is data is available to read.
end − This event is fired when there is no more data to read.
error − This event is fired when there is any error receiving or writing data.
finish − This event is fired when all the data has been flushed to underlying 	system.

﻿ Flask

﻿ Flask       Flask is a lightweight and open-source web framework for Python used to develop web applications and REST APIs. It is called a micro-framework because it provides the essential features needed for web development without forcing a large project structure or many built-in components.

Key Features of Flask
Lightweight: Simple and easy to learn.
Routing: Maps URLs to Python functions using @app.route().
HTTP Methods: Supports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.
Request and Response: Provides objects for handling client requests and server responses.
Templates: Uses Jinja2 for creating dynamic HTML pages.
Cookies and Sessions: Supports storing user-related information.
Extensions: Additional features such as database connectivity and authentication can be added using extensions.
Development Server: Provides a built-in server for testing applications.
